## 2

I appreciate you being upfront about what you believe, but I don’t agree. Even if we set aside every single satellite image and space agency photo, there is an overwhelming amount of evidence you can observe for yourself that only makes sense on a curved, spherical planet.

For example, why do the stars in the night sky change completely as you travel between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres? On a flat plane, you would see the same constellations, just further away or at different angles—yet Polaris disappears entirely once you cross the equator, and the Southern Cross becomes visible. Or consider lunar eclipses: the shadow of the Earth cast onto the Moon is always round, which only a sphere can produce at every angle. 

Questioning official narratives is natural, but the physics of navigation, shadows, and celestial motion have pointed to a globe for thousands of years, long before NASA existed.

## 3

To understand why the sky is blue, you first have to look at what sunlight actually is. 

Even though sunlight looks yellowish-white to us, it’s actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow combined. Light travels in waves, and each color has a different wavelength: red and orange light have long, lazy waves, while blue and violet light have short, tight, choppy waves.

Earth is surrounded by an atmosphere filled with gases—mostly nitrogen and oxygen. When sunlight reaches the atmosphere, the long red and yellow waves pass straight through those tiny gas molecules without hitting much. But the short, choppy blue waves are the exact right size to collide with the air molecules and bounce off in every direction. 

This bouncing around is called *Rayleigh scattering*. Because blue light gets scattered all across the atmosphere, whenever you look up away from the sun, your eyes catch that scattered blue light coming from every corner of the sky. 

(You might wonder why it’s not violet, since violet waves are even shorter! The reason is partly that the sun emits much more blue light than violet, and partly that human eyes are naturally much better at detecting blue.)
